newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Peregrine stung by arrest of Vietnam arm's boss.
newsitem.headline: Peregrine stung by arrest of Vietnam arm's boss.

text.p: Vietnam said on Tuesday it had arrested the head of Peregrine Capital Vietnam on tax evasion charges, dealing a new blow to a company once considered one of the booming economy's most prominent foreign investors.
Australian-Vietnamese businessman Nguyen Trung Truc was arrested on Monday following a lengthy probe into his personal tax affairs, state investigators in Ho Chi Minh City said.
Details of the charges against him were not available, but officials in the southern city said the arrest meant Truc, 44, was likely to face trial within four months.
The investment firm's head office in Hong Kong said it believed the charges related to Truc's personal tax affairs and those of local companies with which he was associated.

"Naturally, we are concerned about Mr Truc and his family and are doing everything we can to assist the Australian consulate in Ho Chi Minh City in its efforts to secure bail for him," Peregrine group's legal counsel Alan Mercer said in a statement.
"Unfortunately, we have not been able to speak to Mr Truc since his arrest," he said.
The company said it had named Judd Kinne, a Singapore-based director on the executive committee of Peregrine Investments, as acting managing director of its Vietnam arm.
Peregrine's sometimes high-profile operations in Vietnam have included investment financing, car sales and liquor distribution.
Truc's arrest marks the latest chapter in a long and bruising saga for the firm that began last May when state investigators turned up, unannounced, at its Ho Chi Minh City offices.

Company officials said at the time it was a routine check. But within weeks a separate tax probe was launched into the affairs of Truc and his Malaysian-Chinese wife, who were barred from leaving Ho Chi Minh City.
In March, local authorities announced fines and punitive steps against the company, while the tax investigation of Truc and several of his family members continued.
It was not immediately clear on Tuesday whether his wife was also being charged.
Australia's ambassador to Vietnam, Susan Boyd, told Reuters that consular officials were in touch with Truc to ensure his legal rights were being upheld. She declined to comment further.

Vietnamese officials have repeatedly sought to play down the impact of the case on other members of its $27 billion foreign investment community, but the affair has coincided with a general erosion of business sentiment.
Investors last year were critical of the high-profile manner in which the case had been conducted, and said Hanoi's decision to take a tough stance with a foreign firm had been ill-timed.
Mercer said Peregrine was winding down its Vietnam operations as a result of the saga and would be focusing on its core banking and investment activities.
"We've been scaling back and we'll be retreating from a distribution business in Vietnam," he said. "Concentrating (instead) on project finance and investment advisory mandates."
Peregrine's troubles are not limited to Vietnam. Recently it protested to the Bangladesh government over an order to arrest the head of a local firm conducting business for Peregrine.
